analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue manufacturers who pressure suppliers to cut off discounting retailers.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill with amendments and bipartisan support, but it never received a Senate floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Sherman Act to make it easier to sue manufacturers that conspire with a retailer's competitors to punish discounters. Under it, if a supplier cut off a reseller after a competitor demanded the reseller stop discounting, a jury could decide whether that was illegal price fixing. It also made any agreement between a supplier and a reseller to set a minimum resale price an automatic antitrust violation, while leaving maximum-price agreements alone. It passed the Senate Judiciary Committee but never came to the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who pay less when retailers compete on price, and discount retailers — including small dealers — who could sue suppliers and competitors' suppliers that cut them off for discounting.

how_it_helps.text: If a supplier cut off a reseller after receiving a competitor's request or demand to curtail price competition, and that demand was the major contributing cause, the case would go to the trier of fact rather than being dismissed by the judge.
Any agreement between a seller and purchaser to set a resale price would be sufficient to constitute a price-fixing violation, with an exception only for agreements to set maximum resale prices.

An agreement between a seller and a purchaser to terminate another dealer or refuse to supply that dealer because of its pricing policies would violate the act even if no specific price level was agreed on.

The bill's own findings state that vertical price restraints generally result in higher consumer prices and that recent court decisions had narrowed the law against them, putting consumer welfare in jeopardy.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and suppliers of branded goods, who could face lawsuits and automatic liability for enforcing minimum resale prices or cutting off dealers over pricing, and who would lose a tool for enforcing service and quality standards.

drawbacks.text: Restricting manufacturers' ability to control dealer pricing could undercut their ability to maintain service, quality, and safety standards — a tradeoff the bill's own findings acknowledge as a manufacturer need it tries to preserve.

The bill reaches implied requests and demands to curb price competition, which critics could argue invites litigation over ordinary business disputes about dealer conduct rather than genuine price fixing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core effect pushes prices toward consumers by making discounting harder to punish, which is a real consumer gain; the cost is that manufacturers lose flexibility to police dealer service and quality, and the bill's broad treatment of 'implied' demands could sweep in ordinary dealer disputes. The carve-out for maximum-price agreements limits one legitimate concern, but the litigation-expanded standard is a genuine tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with amendments and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Metzenbaum on April 19, 1989, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The committee held hearings in June 1989 and ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments in February 1990.
On March 8, 1990, the committee reported the bill to the Senate with amendments and a written report, with additional and minority views filed.
The reported version tightened the cutoff standard so a termination counts only if the competitor's demand was the major contributing cause of the termination.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders but never reached a floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Branded-goods manufacturers and suppliers are better off because the bill died: they kept the ability, under the court decisions of the era, to enforce minimum resale prices and cut off discounting dealers without facing the broader liability the bill would have created. Consumers and discount retailers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Branded-goods manufacturers kept the status quo

for.name: Howard M. Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 30 Senate cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Joseph R. Biden Jr.
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, presided over markup, and reported the bill to the Senate with amendments and a written report.

for.name: 5 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Rudman, Wilson, Boschwitz, Gorton, and others named in the bill text.

against.name: George J. Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; it sat on the legislative calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan: 25 of 55 Senate Democrats and 5 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the Judiciary Committee reported it favorably — though minority views were filed with the committee report.

industries.note: The bill would expose them to lawsuits, and near-automatic liability, for setting minimum resale prices or cutting off dealers over pricing — tools the era's court decisions had largely protected. Their gain from the bill's death was continued freedom to control dealer pricing.
Discounters who get cut off by suppliers after competitor complaints would gain a workable path to sue, protecting their ability to undercut on price. Their interest runs with consumers'.
